summary: Year 5-level vocabulary goal for the Earth–Moon–Sun system: children learn to USE the terms rotation, revolution, axis, tilt, orbit, light year, gravitational force, atmosphere, lunar phases, waxing, waning, solstice, equinox and eclipse correctly inside running explanations of day/night, the seasons and the Moon's phases — not just match words to definitions. Because most terms name dynamic or relational motions and events, and because several form easily-confused pairs (rotation vs revolution; waxing vs waning; solstice vs equinox), each word is best bound to the motion or event it names and the confusable pairs explicitly contrasted. A key moment is applying both words to the SAME Earth so the spin that makes a day (rotation) separates from the lap that makes a year (revolution).
misconceptions: Using 'rotation' and 'revolution' interchangeably — confusing spin (once a day) with orbit (once a year).
Mixing up waxing (growing) and waning (shrinking) for the Moon.
Treating 'orbit' and 'axis' as the same thing, or confusing solstice with equinox.
Thinking a 'light year' is a unit of time rather than distance.
Assuming 'atmosphere' and 'gravitational force' are interchangeable space words rather than distinct concepts.

activities.title: Name-the-motion model: bind each word to what it does
steps: Apply a word to a model of the Earth–Moon–Sun system and watch it perform the motion that word names: choose 'rotation' and see the Earth spin on its axis; choose 'revolution' and see the Earth travel around the Sun.

Apply BOTH 'rotation' and 'revolution' to the SAME Earth, one after the other, and describe out loud the two different motions that play — the spin that makes a day versus the orbit that makes a year.

Apply 'waxing' to a Moon and describe the lit part growing towards full; apply 'waning' and describe the lit part shrinking towards new. Say aloud that the Moon itself is not changing size — only the lit portion we see.
Place 'solstice' and 'equinox' at the correct points on a tilted Earth's year-path and say what each marks (longest or shortest day for a solstice; roughly equal day and night for an equinox).

After each action, say a full sentence that uses the word with the effect it causes, e.g. 'Earth's rotation on its axis causes day and night' and 'Earth's revolution around the Sun, with its tilt, causes the seasons.'
activities.insight: Rotation (spin on the axis, once a day → day and night) and revolution/orbit (travel around the Sun, once a year → the year, and with the tilt the seasons) are two different motions of the same Earth; waxing/waning describe the lit part of the Moon growing/shrinking; solstice/equinox mark day-length events. Each term is bound to a motion or event the child can see and describe.

activities.title: Labelled Earth–Moon–Sun glossary as a companion reference
steps: Explore a labelled Earth–Moon–Sun scene where each term is tagged to its part or motion, revealing an image and a one-line meaning when a term is selected.
Use lift-the-flap or side-by-side panels that put each confusable pair together: rotation beside revolution, waxing beside waning, solstice beside equinox — reading what distinguishes them.
Anchor the scale words to concrete referents: treat 'light year' as a DISTANCE (how far light travels in a year), not a length of time, and 'orbit' as the path one body travels around another.
Use word–phenomenon cards that link each term to what it helps explain: rotation/axis → day and night; tilt/orbit/solstice/equinox → seasons; lunar phases/waxing/waning/eclipse → the Moon.
activities.insight: A consistent reference anchors each term to its part, motion or distance and keeps the confusable pairs visibly distinct, including the correction that a light year measures distance rather than time.

activities.title: Explain day and year in your own words (use-in-context check)
steps: Respond to the prompt: 'Explain what the Earth is doing to make a DAY, and what it's doing to make a YEAR — use the right word for each kind of movement, and tell me what each one causes.'
Show each motion with your body: spin on the spot for rotation; walk a lap around for revolution.

Answer follow-ups that expose conflation: 'You said the Earth revolves — is that the spin that makes a day, or the journey that makes a year?'; 'Tonight the Moon's lit part is bigger than last night — is it waxing or waning?'; 'The longest day of the year — is that a solstice or an equinox? And the day when day and night are equal?'
Transfer the words to a fresh prompt to show the meaning is not tied to one rehearsed sentence.
activities.insight: Asking for use in a running explanation (not a recited definition) reveals whether rotation is pinned to the 24-hour spin and revolution to the yearly orbit, each tied to its effect — exposing the swap a memorised definition would hide.

checkQuestion: Explain to me what the Earth is doing to make a DAY, and what it's doing to make a YEAR — use the right word for each kind of movement, and tell me what each one causes.
checkAnswer: Uses 'rotation' (spin on its axis) for the daily motion that causes day and night, and 'revolution'/'orbit' (travelling round the Sun) for the yearly motion that gives us the year (and, with the tilt, the seasons) — each term applied to the right motion in running explanation, not recited as a definition. Ideally also uses waxing/waning for the Moon growing/shrinking and solstice/equinox for longest-shortest/equal day-length.
